You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. My work involves adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and sending drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back afterwards.
The question: When you arrive at the start of a typical shift, what is the very first thing you do, and how does the rest of your day usually unfold?

Q3
The answer just before it: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, and I handle tasks like adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are ready, and send drones to charge. My notes do not state what the very first thing I do is when I arrive at the start of a shift, or how the rest of my day unfolds.
The question: Who hands work to you during the day, and who do you hand drones or updates over to when you finish a task?

The answer just before it: I don't know.

Q7

The question: What are you most worried a new software service might get wrong or make harder in your work?

Q8
The answer just before it: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. I also worry that the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction may get through twice and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.
The question: Can you give a concrete example of what goes wrong in your work when an instruction gets through twice or a report from a drone arrives late or out of order?

Q10
The answer just before it: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians like me, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you need to show them?

Q11
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You mentioned adding new drones to the fleet and retiring old ones—what happens when you do either of those?

What is involved when you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge?

Q12
The answer just before it: I add new drones to the fleet and retire old ones, and each of our company's drones has a home site. I also set up charging pads at our sites, and we have a few dozen of them which are never lent to another company. Each drone uses a specific charging connector type that is not interchangeable, and I send drones to charge.
The question: What do you need to check or know before you send a drone to charge at one of your sites?

Q13
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What else can you tell me about the drones, the sites, or the charging pads that affects how you do your job?

Q14
The answer just before it: We run a few dozen charging pads at our sites, and they are never lent to another company. Our company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, their sensors, and their charging connectors. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.
The question: What else do you run into with batteries, repairs, or keeping track of drones across your sites?

Q15
The answer just before it: Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Each drone has a home site.
The question: Are there any other constraints or rules about your drones, sites, or charging pads that you have to keep in mind in your work?
